title: Wɔ Hɔn Akyi - At the Doctor's
bridge: In Twi, unlike English, the verb 'to be' is often omitted in the present tense. When describing symptoms or reasons for visiting the doctor, Twi speakers typically use a more direct and concise structure. Additionally, Twi has specific vocabulary for body parts and ailments that may not directly translate to English, so learners should focus on memorizing these terms. Be cautious of word order, as Twi follows a Subject-Object-Verb (SOV) structure, which differs from English's SVO.
rule: To express symptoms or reasons for visiting the doctor in Twi, use the structure: 'Mewu [symptom/reason]' (I have [symptom/reason]). For example, 'Mewu adwene' means 'I have a headache.' When describing body parts, use the possessive pronoun 'me' (my) followed by the body part. For instance, 'Me nsa reme' means 'My hand hurts.' Remember to omit the verb 'to be' in the present tense and focus on the direct translation of symptoms and body parts.

My hand hurts

common_error.explanation: English speakers often directly translate 'I am having' into Twi, but this is incorrect. In Twi, the verb 'to be' is omitted in the present tense, and the structure 'Mewu [symptom]' is used instead. Avoid adding unnecessary verbs and focus on the direct translation of the symptom.

title: Wɔkyerɛ a wɔde ahoɔden no / Booking Accommodation
bridge: In Twi, booking accommodation involves specific phrases and structures that differ from English. Unlike English, Twi uses a more direct approach when asking for availability or prices. Be cautious with word order and the use of pronouns, as Twi often omits subject pronouns when the context is clear. Additionally, Twi has polite forms that are essential in formal conversations, which English speakers might overlook.
rule: To book accommodation in Twi, use the structure 'Mepɛ ahoɔden' (I want accommodation) followed by details like dates or room type. Questions about availability use 'Wohwɛ ahoɔden?' (Do you have accommodation?). Prices are asked with 'Deɛ ahoɔden no, sɛn chi?' (How much is the accommodation?). Polite forms like 'Yɛbɛkyɛ wo' (We will help you) are common in responses. Always use the appropriate tense and ensure clarity in your requests.

title: Sika paa / At the Bank
bridge: In Twi, unlike English, the verb 'to exchange' (siane) is often used for currency exchange, while English uses 'exchange' or 'change'. Twi also uses specific terms for bank roles like 'sika paa' (bank) and 'siane paa' (exchange office), which are more literal than English equivalents. Be cautious with word order in questions, as Twi places the verb after the subject, unlike English.
rule: When discussing money transactions in Twi, use the verb 'siane' for exchanging currency and 'fa' for giving or receiving money. Questions follow the structure: Subject + Verb + Object. For example, 'Wɔ siane sika?' (Do they exchange money?). Always use the appropriate noun for the location: 'sika paa' for bank and 'siane paa' for exchange office.

title: Kwa ho nhia nkyerɛkyerɛ / Job Interview Basics
bridge: In Twi, job interview expressions often involve more indirect and respectful language compared to English. For instance, Twi uses specific verbs and honorifics to show politeness, which can be a trap for English speakers who might directly translate phrases like 'I want this job' without considering the cultural nuance. Additionally, Twi sentences often follow a subject-verb-object (SVO) structure, similar to English, but word order can shift for emphasis, which is less common in English.
rule: When discussing job interviews in Twi, use the verb 'kwa' (to work) with appropriate tenses. Polite expressions like 'Yɛbɛyɛ' (We will do) or 'Mepɛ' (I want) are preferred over direct statements. Honorifics such as 'Onyame' (Sir/Ma'am) or 'Nana' (a respectful title) can be added to address interviewers. Remember, Twi emphasizes respect and humility, so avoid overly assertive language. Typical use cases include expressing skills, asking questions, and thanking the interviewer.

title: Pɔstɔfo mu / At the Post Office
bridge: In Twi, post office interactions often involve specific phrases and structures that differ from English. For instance, Twi uses a more direct approach when asking for services, and the word order can vary. Be cautious with verb conjugations, as Twi verbs don’t change based on the subject like in English. Also, Twi speakers often use polite expressions more frequently than English speakers.
rule: When discussing the post office in Twi, use the phrase 'Me pɛ sɛ...' to express what you want, followed by the service. For example, 'Me pɛ sɛ m’agyea pɔstal' means 'I want to send a letter.' The verb 'agyea' (to send) is commonly used. Polite expressions like 'Yɛfrɛ me' (Please) are often added at the beginning of requests. Remember, Twi sentences typically follow a Subject-Verb-Object (SVO) structure, similar to English, but with fewer verb inflections.

title: Kɔ ahyɛse / Renting a Flat
bridge: In Twi, discussing renting a flat involves specific vocabulary and structures that differ from English. For instance, Twi uses the verb 'kɔ' (to rent) instead of 'rent,' and the noun 'ahyɛse' (flat/apartment) is central. Unlike English, Twi often omits the subject pronoun if the context is clear, which can be a trap for English speakers. Additionally, Twi uses a more direct approach to asking questions, often starting with 'Wɔde...' (Do they rent...) instead of 'Can I rent...'.
rule: To discuss renting a flat in Twi, use the verb 'kɔ' followed by the object 'ahyɛse'. Questions are formed by starting with 'Wɔde...' or 'Mede...' (Do they rent... / Do you rent...). Prices are typically mentioned using 'cedi' (currency) and the verb 'di' (to cost). Be mindful of context when omitting subject pronouns, as Twi relies heavily on situational clarity. For example, 'Mede ahyɛse kɔ?' means 'Do you rent flats?'

title: Kyɛfa / Greetings
bridge: In Twi, greetings are more elaborate and context-dependent than in English. While English speakers often use a simple 'Hi' or 'Hello,' Twi greetings vary based on time of day, social status, and relationship. For example, 'ɛte sɛn?' (Good morning) is specific to mornings, unlike the all-day 'Hello' in English. Avoid directly translating 'How are you?' as Twi speakers often use 'Wo ho te sɛn?' (You're well, right?) as a rhetorical greeting, not expecting a detailed response.
rule: Twi greetings follow a structured pattern: time-based greeting + well-being inquiry. Common greetings include 'ɛte sɛn?' (Good morning), 'ɛda sɛn?' (Good afternoon), and 'ɛkɛsɛ sɛn?' (Good evening). The well-being inquiry 'Wo ho te sɛn?' is often added but requires only a brief 'ɛyɛ' (Yes) or 'yɛ sɛn' (I'm fine) in response. Avoid over-explaining your state unless asked directly with 'Wode aho te sɛn?' (How are you doing?)

(morning), 'ɛda sɛn?' (afternoon), or 'ɛkɛsɛ sɛn?' (evening) followed by 'Wo ho te sɛn?' for politeness, but avoid expecting a detailed response.

title: Adwenee na Mema / Complaining and Apologizing
bridge: In Twi, complaining and apologizing often involve more indirect expressions compared to English. While English speakers might directly say 'I'm sorry' or 'I complain about...', Twi speakers frequently use polite phrases and context-dependent expressions. Be cautious not to overuse direct complaints, as Twi culture values harmony and indirectness. Additionally, apologies in Twi often include explanations or reasons, unlike English where a simple 'sorry' is common.
rule: To complain in Twi, use phrases like 'Mepɛ me ka' (I want to say) followed by the issue. For apologies, 'Mema wo' (Forgive me) or 'Mema me' (Forgive me) are common. Note that 'Mema' is more formal and polite. When apologizing, adding 'Ɛda adi' (It won't happen again) reinforces sincerity. Avoid direct accusations or harsh tones, as Twi culture emphasizes respect and indirect communication.

title: Kɔkɔɔ ne Kɔkɔɔmu / Describing Your Hometown
bridge: In Twi, describing your hometown involves using specific adjectives and structures that differ from English. Unlike English, Twi often places adjectives after the noun, and the language uses a system of noun classes that affects adjective agreement. Be cautious of directly translating English phrases, as Twi expressions for size, location, and atmosphere are unique. For example, 'big town' in English becomes 'kɔkɔɔ bɛyɛ' in Twi, with 'bɛyɛ' meaning 'is big'.
rule: To describe your hometown in Twi, follow these rules: 1) Use the structure 'X yɛ [adjective]' to say 'X is [adjective]'. 2) Adjectives must agree with the noun class of the subject. 3) Use 'wɔ' to indicate location, as in 'wɔ [place]' meaning 'in/at [place]'. 4) For size, use 'bɛyɛ' for 'is big' and 'sɛn’nyɛ' for 'is small'. 5) To describe atmosphere, use phrases like 'yɛ den' for 'is peaceful'. Exceptions include specific idiomatic expressions, which are context-dependent.

title: Nkaeɛ ne Adwuma Mfomso / Talking about Hobbies and Leisure
bridge: In Twi, discussing hobbies often involves the verb 'to do' (kɔ) followed by the noun, unlike English where we typically use 'to' before the verb. Be cautious of word order: Twi places the verb before the object, which is the opposite of English. Additionally, Twi uses specific nouns for hobbies, some of which may not have direct English equivalents, like 'ntɛm' for playing a musical instrument.
rule: To talk about hobbies in Twi, use the structure: 'Me kɔ [noun]' (I do [hobby]). For example, 'Me kɔ ntɛm' (I play a musical instrument). The verb 'kɔ' is irregular and does not change with the subject. When asking about hobbies, use 'Wɔ kɔ dɛn?' (What do you do?) or 'Dɛn na wɔ kɔ?' (What do you do in your free time?). Remember, Twi sentences often omit the subject if it's clear from context.
